workspace.placeholder: Example: We are a two-person content team producing 20 industry articles each week. AI can research and draft, but people must own the point of view, fact-checking, and publishing…
example_values: We are a two-person content team producing 20 industry articles each week. AI should research and draft; people own the point of view, fact-checking, and publishing. Every edit should improve the system.

Our six-person support team handles 500 conversations per day. AI should classify intent, retrieve knowledge, and draft responses; complaints and refunds require human review and corrections become learning data.

Sales reps research new accounts and prepare outreach every day. AI should gather and summarize evidence, reps confirm key judgments, and the system should remember winning messages and failure reasons.

usage.label: How it works
usage.title: From business language to an actionable AI-native operating model
usage.description: Judge first, design second, then stress-test—so AI capability, human accountability, data, and organizational learning form one loop.

items.title: Describe the business goal

items.title: Judge feasibility
items.description: Score task structure, data readiness, externalized judgment, tolerance, and feedback loops.

items.title: Generate the blueprint
items.description: Design roles, Skills, data capture, memory, guardrails, and implementation phases together.

items.title: Stress-test and decide
items.description: Attack the design with failure cases, then let people resolve the remaining decisions.

features.label: Capabilities
features.title: Built to make AI-native work real
features.description: More than prompts or a demo: an operating blueprint your team can pilot, validate, and continuously improve.

items.title: Feasibility first
items.description: Know whether the use case is worth doing and what must be fixed before a pilot.

items.title: Human–AI accountability
items.description: Define what AI does, what people own, the handoff artifact, and acceptance criteria.

items.title: Skills and triggers
items.description: Turn one-off prompts into reusable capabilities with defined inputs, outputs, and activation rules.

items.title: Data and memory design
items.description: Plan what to capture during work, where memory reads and writes, and how it stays clean and current.

items.title: Adversarial quality checks
items.description: Create guardrails and tests for hallucination, cold start, missing data, and accountability gaps.

items.title: Actionable rollout plan
items.description: Break the blueprint into pilot, evaluation, and scale phases with measurable success criteria.

faq.label: FAQ
faq.title: What teams ask before they build
faq.description: Clear answers about AI-native blueprints, human accountability, and data safety.

items.title: How is AI-native different from using an AI tool?
items.description: A tool solves one task. An AI-native system redesigns roles, Skills, data, and memory so the operating model improves through feedback.

items.title: What does 'not ready' mean?
items.description: It is not a permanent rejection. It means current information, tolerance, or feedback conditions are insufficient; the blueprint lists the blockers and fixes.

items.title: Do I need technical expertise?
items.description: No. Business owners describe the goal and decide critical boundaries; technical teams connect real data and tools during implementation.

items.title: Can the blueprint go straight to production?
items.description: It is an implementation-ready design input, not an untested production system. Start with a small pilot using real samples and human acceptance.

items.title: How is business information handled?
items.description: Your description is used for this model analysis and never needs passwords or API keys. Sensitive connections belong in secure credential systems during implementation.
